name: GHRP-1

lead: GHRP-1 is one of the first synthetic growth hormone releasing peptides, developed alongside GHRP-6 and GHRP-2. People look to it for higher growth hormone, which they connect to more muscle and less body fat.

It binds the ghrelin/GH secretagogue receptor, separate from the GHRH receptor, and prompts growth hormone release. A 1993 review reported that it, GHRP-6 and GHRP-2 were the three such peptides given to humans, and that all released more GH than GHRH 1-44. Studies measured hormone release; body-composition outcomes have not been tested.

paras: It is discussed in peptide and bodybuilding communities as one of the older GHRPs, usually in the context of a muscle-building or fat-loss plan. It was largely superseded by later peptides.
It is a research peptide, not an approved medicine, and little modern human safety data exists. It is prohibited in sport, and anti-doping labs have developed urine tests for it and its metabolites.

angle.text: GHRP-1 is grouped with GHRP-6 and GHRP-2 as a way to raise growth hormone for muscle gain and fat loss. It stimulates GH release through the ghrelin receptor, and some 1990s human work measured that release.

lead: GHRP-1 (growth hormone releasing peptide-1) is a synthetic heptapeptide from the first family of growth hormone releasing peptides (GHRPs), which also includes GHRP-6, GHRP-2 and hexarelin. These small peptides prompt the pituitary to release growth hormone (GH) through a receptor distinct from the one used by growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH).[1][2]

The appearance interest in the class follows a chain: more GH release -> higher IGF-1 signalling -> changes in body composition, such as leaner mass and less fat. People in muscle-building circles discuss GHRP-6 and GHRP-2 far more often than GHRP-1, and the same reasoning is applied to the whole family.[3] Published research on GHRP-1 itself is mostly pharmacology from the early 1990s and later reviews of the class.[1][4]

A 1993 review reported that GHRP-6, GHRP-1 and GHRP-2 were the three such peptides given to humans, in increasing order of effectiveness, and that all released more growth hormone than GHRH 1-44.[2] GHRP-1 is not approved as a medicine. Anti-doping laboratories have developed urine tests for it and its metabolites.[5]

paras: GHRP-1 is a seven-amino-acid peptide, which makes it a heptapeptide, whereas GHRP-6, GHRP-2 and hexarelin are hexapeptides.[1][6] A 1998 review lists the family as hepta- (GHRP-1) and hexapeptides (GHRP-2, GHRP-6, hexarelin), and notes that non-peptide secretagogues such as MK-0677 were later discovered using GHRP-6 as a template.[6]

Reviews describe GHRP-1 as one of the 'superanalogues' developed after GHRP-6, the first hexapeptide to be studied extensively in humans.[1][7] Their GH-releasing activity was described as marked, dose related and reproducible after intravenous, subcutaneous, intranasal and even oral administration, with partial desensitization on prolonged use.[7]

GHRPs have no structural homology with GHRH and act at specific receptors in the pituitary and hypothalamus, later identified as the ghrelin receptor.[1] Wikipedia lists GHRP-1 among the synthetic agonists of this receptor. Reviews note that the cloned receptor suggested the existence of a natural GHRP-like ligand; the ghrelin receptor was later matched to that role.[1]

Several hypotheses were proposed for how GHRPs act: counteracting somatostatin at the pituitary and hypothalamus, partial action through GHRH, or an unidentified hypothalamic factor.[1] A controlled 1992 study in five healthy men found that the GH response to a GHRP persisted when the response to GHRH had been abolished by prolonged GHRH infusion, concluding that the response does not depend on endogenous GHRH.[8]

The class also releases prolactin and ACTH/cortisol to a degree, and influences food intake and sleep pattern, according to a 2000 review. Receptors for GHRPs were found in heart, adrenal, ovary, testis, lung and skeletal muscle at densities higher than in the hypothalamic-pituitary system, and binding to human cardiac membranes was inhibited by GHRP-1 among other peptides.[9]

Human studies of GHRP-1 are from the early 1990s: reviews describe it among the peptides administered to people.[2] Related GHRP work in healthy men includes controlled studies showing GH release after intravenous GHRP and after oral GHRP in a single-blind randomized design, and studies of prolonged infusion and its effect on pulsatile GH secretion.[4][8][10] Another randomized study examined GH responses to a GHRP in GH-deficient children and compared them with GHRH.[11]

A 1998 review of secretagogues in thalassemia, where GH secretion can be subnormal, described GHRP-1 among agents that can be given by several routes and considered them candidates where GH secretion is reduced but the pituitary is intact.[12]

One phase 2 trial of a GHRP-1 formulation (GHRP-1/AG) in end-stage renal disease patients on hemodialysis was registered in 2006 and terminated with three participants.[13] Animal work in rats examined GHRP-1, -2, -6 and hexarelin in heart failure and cachexia.[14] No published trial has tested GHRP-1 for body composition or appearance in healthy people.

GHRPs are on the lists of substances prohibited in sport, and analytical methods exist to detect GHRP-1 and its metabolites in urine.[5][15] Doping-control researchers have noted that the standard test for exogenous GH does not detect these peptides, which is why dedicated assays were developed.[5]

On forums such as T Nation, discussion of the class centres on GHRP-6 and GHRP-2, often combined with other peptides, with members debating how their effects compare with GH itself; one poster reported water gain rather than muscle from GH-related compounds.[3] GHRP-1 is rarely named in those threads.
